result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.find_induced_nodes()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Find the nodes on induced paths between two nodes of a chordal graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.find_induced_nodes()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: >- Find the nodes on induced paths between two nodes of a chordal graph. title: >- [Graph.find_induced_nodes()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Find the nodes on induced paths between two nodes of a chordal graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the nodes on induced paths between two nodes of a chordal graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L31999-L32065){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.find_induced_nodes( source, target, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Find induced nodes](../assets/graphs/find-induced-nodes.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A path A, B, C, D, a tree and so chordal, queried from A to D (both outlined). The dashed accent arc is the hypothetical edge A to D: it would close the cycle A, B, C, D, so every node on the induced path between them is returned. B and C are in the accent color and the card lists [A, B, C, D]." width="100%"} In a chordal graph, this returns the nodes lying on induced paths (paths with no shortcuts) between `source` and `target`: the nodes that would join a cycle with `source` and `target` if the edge `source`-`target` were added. They identify which variables become connected when two variables are linked in a triangulated graphical model. When `source` and `target` are adjacent, or no induced path of length two or more exists, the result is empty. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The first node, as an ID or label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second node, as an ID or label. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node IDs found, sorted (always including `target` when not empty). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, not chordal, or a node does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Following NetworkX's `find_induced_nodes`: the edge `source`-`target` is added, and maximum cardinality searches from `source` repeatedly find a chordless triple, whose nodes are joined to `source` until the graph is chordal again. When several missing edges could complete a triple, EdgeCase takes the one with the lowest node IDs while NetworkX follows Python's set order, so on some graphs the two return different (equally valid) node sets; whether the result is empty never differs. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a path A-B-C-D (a tree, hence chordal), the induced path from A to D is the whole path: ::: {#08a22e55 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) path.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")]) [path.get_label_from_id(n) for n in path.find_induced_nodes("A", "D")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'] ``` ::: :::
